passages.title: Cyrus permits return
passages.summary: Cyrus announces temple rebuilding. Families prepare to return, and Sheshbazzar receives the temple vessels.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · Persian reign sequence requires comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected known places and broad regions. Ahava, Casiphia, and the archive destination are not assigned unsupported coordinates.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies how people outside the community can help God’s work.

contextNote.title: Return occurs within Persian rule
contextNote.text: Permission to rebuild comes from the king who rules the larger region. The people return with help, goods, and temple vessels. Worship can resume without political independence. Read permission and dependence together. The Cyrus Cylinder provides wider royal context without naming Judah’s returning families.

passages.title: The returning community
passages.summary: A list names returning families and temple workers. Some priests must prove their family line.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · Persian reign sequence requires comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected known places and broad regions. Ahava, Casiphia, and the archive destination are not assigned unsupported coordinates.

lds.text: The Seminary introduction describes the families returning from exile, or forced life abroad. What do their gifts help rebuild?

contextNote.title: Belonging requires more than arrival
contextNote.text: The list distinguishes households, workers, and claims to priestly service. Missing family records restrict access to sacred food. A rebuilt temple therefore needs decisions about membership as well as materials. The returning group must establish who can perform each task.

passages.title: Altar, foundations, joy, and grief
passages.summary: Jeshua and Zerubbabel lead renewed offerings and temple work. The foundation ceremony brings both celebration and grief.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · Persian reign sequence requires comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected known places and broad regions. Ahava, Casiphia, and the archive destination are not assigned unsupported coordinates.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me considers the joy and grief accompanying temple rebuilding.

contextNote.title: A foundation holds two different memories
contextNote.text: The same ceremony produces joy in some people and grief in others. Older witnesses compare the new work with a lost temple. Their tears do not cancel the other people's celebration. The account preserves both responses within the sound of one gathering.

passages.title: Opposition and royal letters
passages.summary: An offer of help is rejected. Opposition and letters to Persian rulers interrupt rebuilding before work resumes under Darius.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · Persian reign sequence requires comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected known places and broad regions. Ahava, Casiphia, and the archive destination are not assigned unsupported coordinates.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies responses to opposition.

contextNote.title: Opposition does not follow a simple sequence
contextNote.text: The chapter groups disputes from several reigns before returning to temple work under Darius. Some letters concern the city rather than the temple. Read each royal name and building request carefully. A shared theme of opposition holds together events from different times.

passages.title: Prophets encourage work as officials ask questions
passages.summary: Haggai and Zechariah encourage rebuilding. Tattenai asks for proof of Cyrus's order, and the leaders explain their work.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · Persian reign sequence requires comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected known places and broad regions. Ahava, Casiphia, and the archive destination are not assigned unsupported coordinates.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks how the people continue God’s work despite opposition.

contextNote.title: Local builders answer through a longer history
contextNote.text: The elders identify themselves as servants before explaining their building work. Their answer connects royal permission with earlier destruction and return. They admit ancestral failure without accepting that rebuilding lacks authority. The dispute concerns who can authorize work within the empire.

passages.title: The king's order, the temple, and Passover
passages.summary: The archive search supports rebuilding. Darius supplies protection and resources. The community dedicates the temple and celebrates Passover.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · Persian reign sequence requires comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected known places and broad regions. Ahava, Casiphia, and the archive destination are not assigned unsupported coordinates.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the temple's opening and the people's joy.

contextNote.title: A stored record changes a local dispute
contextNote.text: The search for a decree moves the dispute into royal archives. A written record can answer claims made by local opponents. Permission also brings duties and royal oversight. The temple story therefore includes files, officials, and taxes. The rebuilt community remains inside a larger system of rule.

passages.title: Ezra studies the law and receives royal support
passages.summary: Ezra is a priest who studies God’s law. Artaxerxes supports his journey and gives him duties to teach and judge.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · Persian reign sequence requires comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected known places and broad regions. Ahava, Casiphia, and the archive destination are not assigned unsupported coordinates.

lds.text: The Church lesson joins scripture study with practice and teaching.

contextNote.title: Teaching joins study with conduct
contextNote.text: Ezra's description places study before practice and teaching. The royal letter then connects instruction with courts and public penalties. Law functions here as more than private guidance. Its teachers receive power over how the community orders its life.

passages.title: Prayer, travel, and the care of temple gifts
passages.summary: Ezra gathers travelers and asks Iddo to send temple workers. They pray before leaving and count the gifts when they arrive.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · Persian reign sequence requires comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected known places and broad regions. Ahava, Casiphia, and the archive destination are not assigned unsupported coordinates.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson studies fasting, prayer, and trust before the journey.

contextNote.title: Sacred gifts need public accountability
contextNote.text: Ezra's trust in protection does not remove the need to weigh the gifts. Selected guardians receive them before travel and deliver them after arrival. The matching weights make responsibility visible to others. Prayer and careful handling serve the same journey.

passages.title: Ezra prays about the mixed marriages
passages.summary: Leaders report marriages with women from other nations. Ezra tears his robe and begins a prayer.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · Persian reign sequence requires comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected known places and broad regions. Ahava, Casiphia, and the archive destination are not assigned unsupported coordinates.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects these marriages with worship of other gods. Ezra gives no personal testimony from the wives.

contextNote.title: Gratitude and fear shape the prayer
contextNote.text: Ezra describes renewed life as a small allowance within continued foreign rule. That limited recovery explains his fear of losing the community again. The prayer interprets present marriages through the memory of exile. It expresses Ezra's judgment, not the voices of the affected wives.

passages.title: The marriage investigation
passages.summary: Shecaniah proposes separation from foreign wives and children. Ezra summons an assembly, and an investigation names households involved.
passages.dateLabel: Chapter order · Persian reign sequence requires comparison
passages.uncertainty: Selected known places and broad regions. Ahava, Casiphia, and the archive destination are not assigned unsupported coordinates.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson studies confession and repentance. What voices are missing from the account of separated families?

contextNote.title: A boundary decision has a human cost
contextNote.text: The proposed covenant requires wives and children to leave. The account names this as a response to unfaithfulness. Its focus on group identity does not remove the cost for families. Read the named men beside those affected but largely unheard. A return to worship does not settle every question about belonging.
